\label{lem:Jn_min_primes}
With the setup as in \ref{setup:Jn}, we have that the following ideals are minimal primes of $J_{G}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $P_{i,i+2}$ for $2 \leq i \leq 2n+3$, and
\item $Q_{i}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 3$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-21 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The proof that $P_{i,i+2}$ is a minimal prime of $J_{G}$ is analogous to the proof in Lemma \ref{lem:minimal_primes_anti_hole}.
    \item We show that $Q_{1}$ is a minimal prime of $J_{G}$. First, we observe that if $S := \{j \mid 2 \leq j \leq 2n+3\} \cup \{2n+7\}$, then $G \smallsetminus S$ consists of two connected components $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ where $V(G_{1}) = \{1,2n+4,2n+6\}$ and $E(G_{1}) = \{ \{1,2n+6\}, \{2n+4,2n+6\} \}$, and $G_{2}$ is the graph on the singleton vertex $\{2n+5\}$. It is clear that $S$ is a cut set of $G$, and hence $Q_{1}$ is a minimal prime of $J_{G}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:min_primes_binomial_edge_ideal}. Similarly, it is shown that $Q_{2}$ is a minimal prime of $J_{G}$. 
    \item We show that $Q_{3}$ is a minimal prime of $J_{G}$. If $S = \{2n+6,2n+7\}$, then $G \smallsetminus S$ consists of two connected components. The set $G_{1}$ on the vertex set $1$, and $G_{2}$ on the vertices $\{j \mid 2 \leq j \leq 2n+5\}$. Adding $2n+6$ or $2n+7$ reconnects these connected components, and it follows that $S$ is a cut set of $G$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lem-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:colon_minimal_primes_Jn}
With the setup as in \ref{setup:Jn}, we have that
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $2 \leq i \leq 2n+3$ that 
\begin{align*}
    P_{i,i+2}^{[2]} : J_{G} = P_{i,i+2}^{[2]} + (f_{i,i+2} \, \omega_{A})
\end{align*}
\item For $i = 1,2$ we have that 
\begin{align*}
    Q_{i}^{[2]}:J_{G} = Q_{i}^{[2]} + L_{Q_{i}}.
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-22 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Follows from Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime}. When applying Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime} to $Q_{1}$, we let $a = 2n+4$, $b = 2n+5$, $c = 2n+6$, and $d = 1$. When applying Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime} to $Q_{2}$, we let $a = 3$, $b = 2$, $c = 2n+7$, and $d = 1$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn_degree_two_monomial_in_Supp}
With the setup as in \ref{setup:Jn}, let $r \in J$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, then either
\begin{align*}
\frac{x_{1}y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \quad \text{ or }  \quad \frac{x_{1}y_{5}}{y_{1}x_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
\item If $m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, then 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{1}y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{1}y_{5}}{y_{1}x_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
First we observe that Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} applied to $P_{3,5}$ where $p = x_{1}$ and $q = y_{1}$ implies that
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{1}y_{3}}{y_{1}x_{3}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{1}y_{5}}{y_{1}x_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
Repeatedly applying Lemma~\ref{lem:cycling} we get the following
\begin{align*}
    \frac{y_{1}x_{3}}{x_{1}y_{3}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
    &\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2n+5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} \text{ via } Q_{1}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2}x_{3}}{x_{2}y_{3}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{1}y_{2}}{y_{1}x_{2}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} \text{ via } Q_{2}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{1}y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ via } P_{2,4}).
\end{align*}
The statement now follows from Lemma \ref{lem:Jn_m_in_Supp_f} applied to $Q_{2}$ as we have that 
\begin{align*}
    \left \lvert  \left\{ \frac{y_{1}x_{3}}{x_{1}y_{3}} \cdot m, \frac{x_{1}y_{3}}{y_{1}x_{3}} \cdot m, m\right \} \cap \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \right\rvert \equiv 0 \mod{2}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn_cycling_xi_by_yi}
With the setup as in \ref{setup:Jn}, let $r \in J$. If 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn_cycling_xi_by_yi_1}
    \frac{x_{i}}{y_{i}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \quad  (\text{respectively, } \frac{y_{i}}{x_{i}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) )
\end{equation}
for some $i \in \{1,4,5\}$, then the same holds for all $i \in \{1,4,5\}$.
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} applied to $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{2n+4}}{y_{2n+4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \text{ and } \frac{x_{3}}{y_{3}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r),
\end{align*}
respectively. Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that 
\begin{align*}
\frac{x_{2n+4}}{y_{2n+4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \text{ and } \frac{x_{3}}{y_{3}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
\end{align*}
if and only if 
\begin{align*}
\frac{x_{4}}{y_{4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \text{ and } \frac{x_{5}}{y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r),
\end{align*}
respectively.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- cor-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn_restrictions_elements_in_support_of_colon}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn}. If $r \in J$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, then 
\begin{align*}
    r' \notin \left\{ \frac{x_{i}}{x_{1}y_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{x_{1}y_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{x_{i}}{y_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{x_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m \right\}_{i=4,5}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end cor-7 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} it follows for $r \in \bigcap_{i=1,2} (Q_{i}^{[2]}:J_{G})$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ that 
\begin{align*}
    r' \notin \left\{ \frac{x_{i}}{x_{1}y_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{x_{1}y_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{x_{i}}{y_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{x_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m \right\}_{i=3,2n+4}.
\end{align*}
The claim now follows by applying Lemma \ref{lem:cycling}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- cor-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:restrictions_supp_r}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn}. If $r \in J$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, then
\begin{align*}
    r' \notin \left\{ \frac{x_{i}}{x_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{y_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m, \right \}_{i=4,5} \cup \left \{ \frac{1}{y_{1}} \cdot m, \frac{1}{x_{1}} \cdot m \right \}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end cor-8 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:elt_in_supp_r}
    \frac{x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{5}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2n+5}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r)
\end{equation}
Lemma \ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} applied to $Q_{1}$ with $p = x_{2n+5}$, $q = y_{2n+5}$, $a = 1$, $c = 2n+4$, and $d = 2n+6$ implies that equation \eqref{eqn:elt_in_supp_r} is equivalent to 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_2}
    \frac{x_{2n+5}}{y_{2n+5}}\cdot  \frac{y_{2n+6}}{y_{1}x_{2n+6}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{equation}
Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that equation \eqref{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_2} is equivalent to 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_3}
    \frac{1}{y_{1}} \cdot \frac{y_{2}x_{3}}{x_{2}y_{3}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{equation}
Now, Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied via $Q_{2}$ with $a = 3$, $c =1$, $d = 2n+7$, $p = y_{2}$, and $q = x_{2}$ implies equation \eqref{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_3}. A similar argument shows that
\begin{align*}
    r' \notin \left \{\frac{x_{i}}{x_{1}y_{i}} \cdot m, \frac{y_{i}}{y_{1}x_{i}} \cdot m, \right \}_{i=4,5}.
\end{align*}

Lemma \ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} applied via $Q_{1}$ shows that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{y_{1}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}y_{2n+4}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_4}
\begin{aligned}
    \frac{x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}y_{2n+4}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \iff \frac{x_{4}}{x_{1}y_{4}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Equation \eqref{eqn:elt_in_supp_r_4} has been previously established in this proof. A similar argument proves that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{x_{1}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lem-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:jn_leftover_elements_not_killed_modulo_ideal}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn}. We denote by $S$ the set of squarefree monomials of degree $2$ on the variables $\{x_{i},y_{i} \mid i = 1,4,5\}$. Define the ideals
\begin{align*}
    \mathfrak{a}_{0} &:= (\{x_{j}^{2},y_{j}^{2}\}_{j=6}^{2n+7}) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{1} &:= (x_{2}^{2},y_{2}^{2},x_{3}^{2},y_{3}^{2}) + ( \{x_{j}^{3}, y_{j}^{3}\}_{j=1,4,5} ) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{2} &:= ( S \smallsetminus  \{x_{1}y_{4}, x_{1}y_{5}\} )^{[2]} \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{3} &:= ( \{ x_{j}^{2}y_{j}, y_{j}^{2}x_{j}\}_{j = 1,4,5} ),
\end{align*}
and $L := \sum_{i=1}^{3} \mathfrak{a}_{i}$. Let $r \in J$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$. If $r' \notin L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, then $r'$ belongs to the following set:
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{A}_{1}\cup \mathcal{A}_{2} \cup \mathcal{A}_{3}, 
\end{align*}
where $\mathcal{A}_{i} := \{h_{i,1},h_{i,2},h_{i,3}\}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 3$ and
\begin{align*}
    h_{1,1} &:= \frac{x_{1}y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}} \cdot m 
    & h_{1,2} &:= \frac{x_{1}y_{5}}{y_{1}x_{5}} \cdot m
    & h_{1,3} &:= 1\cdot m  \\
    h_{2,1} &:= \frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}} \cdot m 
    & h_{2,2} &:= \frac{x_{4}}{y_{4}} \cdot m
    & h_{2,3} &:= \frac{x_{5}}{y_{5}} \cdot m  \\
    h_{3,1} &:= \frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}} \cdot m     
    & h_{3,2} &:= \frac{y_{4}}{x_{4}} \cdot m 
    & h_{3,3} &:= \frac{y_{5}}{x_{5}} \cdot m.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lem-23 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
We have that
\begin{align*}
    r \in \bigcap_{i=3,4} P_{i,i+2}^{[2]}:J_{G}.
\end{align*}
Since $r' \notin L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} implies that $\omega_{S} \mid r'$ for $S = [2n+7] \smallsetminus \{1,4,5\}$.

\underline{Case 1}. Suppose that $r'$ is not divisible by $x_{i}^{2}$ nor by $y_{i}^{2}$ for $i = 4,5$. Then, Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} applied to $Q_{1}$ implies that  $\omega_{T} \mid r'$ where $T = [2n+7] \smallsetminus \{1\}$, and that $x_{1} \mid r'$ or that $y_{1} \mid r'$. Thus, we have that
\begin{align*}
    r'  = \frac{d'}{x_{1}y_{1}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some $d' \in \{x_{1},y_{1},x_{1}y_{1},x_{1}^{2},y_{1}^{2}\}$. 
Corollary \ref{cor:restrictions_supp_r} implies that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $d' = x_{1}y_{1}$, in which case $r' = h_{1,3}$,
\item $d' = x_{1}^{2}$, in which case $r' = h_{2,1}$.
\item $d' = y_{1}^{2}$, in which case $r' = h_{3,1}$.
\end{enumerate}

\underline{Case 2}. Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $x_{4}^{2}$. Then $r'$ is not divisible by $y_{i}^{2}$ for $i=1,4,5$, $x_{1}^{2}$, or $x_{5}^{2}$ (otherwise, $r' \in \mathfrak{a}_{2}$). The requirement that
\begin{equation}
	\label{eqn:Jn_r'_divisibility_1}
    r \in P_{2,4}^{[2]} : J_{G}
\end{equation}
implies via Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} that $x_{5}y_{5} \mid r'$. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' x_{4}}{x_{1}y_{1}y_{4}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \in \{1,x_{1},y_{1},x_{1}y_{1}\}$. (We notice that $y_{4} \nmid d'$; otherwise, $r' \in \mathfrak{a}_{3}$.) Corollaries \ref{cor:Jn_restrictions_elements_in_support_of_colon} and \ref{cor:restrictions_supp_r} imply that $d' = x_{1}y_{1}$, and thus that $r' = h_{2,2}$.

\underline{Case 3}. Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $x_{5}^{2}$. This case is similar to case 2, and we find that $r' = h_{2,3}$.

\underline{Case 4}. Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $y_{4}^{2}$. As in case 2 we have that 
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' y_{4}}{x_{1}y_{1}x_{4}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $d' \in \{1,x_{1},y_{1},x_{1}y_{1},x_{1}^{2} \}$. Corollary \ref{cor:Jn_restrictions_elements_in_support_of_colon} implies that $d' = x_{1}y_{1}$ (in which case $r' = h_{3,2}$) or that $d' = x_{1}^{2}$ (in which case $r' = h_{1,1}$).

\underline{Case 5.} Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $y_{5}^{2}$. This case is similar to case 4, and we find that $r' = h_{1,2}$ or that $r' = h_{3,3}$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:Jn_J_contained_in_Q}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn}, and let $L$ and $\mathfrak{a}_{0}$ be defined as in Lemma \ref{lem:jn_leftover_elements_not_killed_modulo_ideal}. Then, 
\begin{align*}
    J + L + \mathfrak{a}_{0} \subseteq (h_{1,1} + h_{1,3},h_{1,2}+h_{1,3},h_{2,1}+h_{2,2}+h_{2,3},h_{3,1}+h_{3,2}+h_{3,3}) + L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Let $r \in J$. Let $S := \operatorname{Supp}(r) \smallsetminus (L + \mathfrak{a}_{0})$. Define the sets
\begin{align*}
    S_{1} &= \{h_{1,1},h_{1,3}\} \\
    S_{2} &= \{h_{1,2},h_{1,3}\} \\
    S_{3} &= \{h_{1,1},h_{1,2}\} \\
    S_{4} &= \{h_{2,1},h_{2,2},h_{2,3}\} \\
    S_{5} &= \{h_{3,1},h_{3,2},h_{3,3}\}.
\end{align*}
Corollaries \ref{cor:Jn_degree_two_monomial_in_Supp} and \ref{cor:Jn_cycling_xi_by_yi} and Lemma \ref{lem:jn_leftover_elements_not_killed_modulo_ideal} imply that there exists $1 \leq t \leq 5$ and $1 \leq i_{1} < \cdots < i_{t} \leq 5$ satisfying $\# \left( \{i_{1},\ldots,i_{t}\} \cap \{1,2,3\} \right) \leq 1$ such that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn_reln_1}
    S = S_{i_{1}} \sqcup \cdots \sqcup S_{i_{t}}.
\end{equation}
It follows that
\begin{align*}
    r = \sum_{j = 1}^{t} \sum_{g\in S_{i_{j}}} g \mod{(L + \mathfrak{a}_{0})}.
\end{align*}
For $1 \leq i \leq 5$ we have that 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{g\in S_{i}} g \in (h_{1,1} + h_{1,3},h_{1,2}+h_{1,3},h_{2,1}+h_{2,2}+h_{2,3},h_{3,1}+h_{3,2}+h_{3,3}),
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- thrm-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:Jn_not_F_pure}
Let $n \geq 0$ be a positive integer, and $G$ the graph $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_1^{2n+3}$. Then $J_{G}$ is not F-pure.
<!-- end thrm-11 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
When $n = 0$, it can be verified via Macaulay2 that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure. Hence, it suffices to consider the case $n \geq 1$. We utilize the notation for $h_{i,j}$ and $L$ as they are defined in \ref{lem:jn_leftover_elements_not_killed_modulo_ideal}. We will use Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} to prove that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure. Adopting the notation from Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} we have that $A = \{2n+6,2n+7\}$, $B = [2n+7] \smallsetminus (A\cup \{1\})$, $Q = P(A,B)$, $m = 5$, $B' = [5] \smallsetminus \{1\}$, $Q' = P(\varnothing,B')$. We define the ideal
\begin{align*}
    K := (h_{1,1} + h_{1,3},h_{1,2}+h_{1,3},h_{2,1}+h_{2,2}+h_{2,3},h_{3,1}+h_{3,2}+h_{3,3}) + L.
\end{align*}
We define $\mathcal{ C } := \{P_{i,i+2} \mid 2 \leq i \leq 2n+3\}\cup \{Q_{i} \mid i \in \{1,2\}\}$. Proposition \ref{prop:Jn_J_contained_in_Q} implies that the containment \eqref{eqn:reduction_step_fedder_computation_assumption_1} of Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} is satisfied. We verify using Macaulay2 that the containment \eqref{eqn:reduction_step_fedder_computation_assumption_2} of Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} is satisfied. Thus, Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} implies that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\label{defn:Jn1}
For $n \geq 0$, $\mathrm{XF}_5^{2n+3}$ denotes the graph on $2n+8$ vertices having edge set 
\begin{align*}
\{ &\{1,i\}_{i = 3}^{2n+6}, \{2,i\}_{i = 3}^{2n+6}, \{i,i+1\}_{i=2}^{2n+5}, \{2, 2n+7\}, \{2n+6, 2n+7\},\\
&\{1,2n+8\}, \{3,2n+8\} \}.
\end{align*}
Then, $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_5^{2n+3} := \overline{\mathrm{XF}_5^{2n+3}}$.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- thrm-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:Jn1_not_F_pure}
Let $n \geq 0$ be a positive integer, and $G$ the graph $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_5^{2n+3}$. Then, $J_{G}$ is not F-pure.
<!-- end thrm-12 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
After completing $G$ at the vertex $1$ we have that vertex $2$ is connected to the vertices $2n+7$ and $2n+8$. Now, the induced subgraph of $G$ on the vertices $[2n+8] \smallsetminus \{1\}$ is isomorphic to the graph $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_1^{2n+3}$. As $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_1^{2n+3}$ is not F-pure for $n\geq 0$ (Theorem \ref{thm:Jn_not_F_pure}), it follows that $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_5^{2n+3}$ is not F-pure by Lemma \ref{lem:F_split_descends_to_induced_subgraph}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
\label{defn:Jn2}
For $n \geq 0$, $\mathrm{XF}_6^{2n+2}$ denotes the graph on $2n+7$ vertices having edge set 
\begin{align*}
\{ \{1,i\}_{i = 2}^{2n+5}, \{2,i\}_{i = 3}^{2n+5}, \{i,i+1\}_{i=2}^{2n+4}, \{2,2n+6\}, \{2n+5,2n+6\}, \{1, 2n+7\}, \{3, 2n+7\} \}.
\end{align*}
Then, $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{2n+2} := \overline{\mathrm{XF}_6^{2n+2}}$
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
The labeling of the vertices in defining $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{2n+2}$ in Definition \ref{defn:Jn2} is different than the labeling of the vertices as defined in Trotter \cite{trotter1992combinatorics}.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- setup-5: body_md -->
\label{setup:Jn2}
By $n$ we denote a positive integer greater than or equal to $2$.\footnote{We will treat the cases of $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{2}$ and $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{4}$ separately.} We denote by $G$ the graph $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{2n+2}$. For $3 \leq i \leq 2n+3$, we denote by $P_{i,i+2}$ the ideal
\begin{align*}
    P_{i,i+2} := P([2n+7]\smallsetminus\{1,2,i,i+1,i+2\},\{i,i+2\}).
\end{align*}
We define the ideals
\begin{align*}
Q_{1} &:= P(\{ j \mid 5 \leq j \leq 2n+6 \}, \{2,4,2n+7\}) \\
Q_{2} &:= P( \{j \mid 3 \leq j \leq 2n+3 \text{ or } j = 2n+7 \}, \{1,2n+4,2n+6\} ) \\
Q_{3} &:= P(\{2n+6,2n+7\}, \{ 3 \leq j \leq 2n+5 \} ).
\end{align*}
We denote by $J$ the ideal 
\begin{align*}
    J := \bigcap_{i=3}^{2n+3} \left( P_{i,i+2}^{[2]}:J_{G} \right) \bigcap \bigcap_{i=1,2} \left( Q_{i}^{[2]}:J_{G} \right).
\end{align*}
We denote by $m$ the monomial
\begin{align*}
    m &:= \prod_{j=1}^{2n+7} x_{j}y_{j}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end setup-5 -->
<!-- lem-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:jn2_min_primes}
With setup as in \ref{setup:Jn2}, we have that the following ideals are minimal primes of $J_{G}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $P_{i,i+2} := \left( f_{i,i+2},\{x_{j},y_{j}\}_{j\in[2n+7] \smallsetminus \{ 1,2,i,i+1,i+2 \}} \right)$ where $3 \leq i \leq 2n+3$, and
\item $Q_{i}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 3$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-24 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Jn_min_primes}
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lem-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:colon_minl_primes_J_n_2}
With setup as in \ref{setup:Jn2}, we have that
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $3 \leq i \leq 2n+3$,
\begin{align*}
P_{i,i+2}^{[2]}:J_{G} = P_{i,i+2} + (f_{i,i+2} \, \omega_{A}).
\end{align*}
\item For $i = 1,2$, we have that
\begin{align*}
Q_{i}^{[2]}:J_{G} = Q_{i}^{[2]} + L_{Q_{i}}.
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-25 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Follows from Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime}. When applying Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime} to $Q_{1}$, we let $a = 4$, $b = 3$, $c = 2n+7$, and $d = 2$. When applying Theorem \ref{thrm:colon_minl_prime} to $Q_{2}$, we let $a = 2n+4$, $b = 2n+5$, $c = 2n+6$, and $d = 1$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- cor-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn2_restrictions_supp_r}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. If $r \in J$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, then
\begin{align*}
    r' \notin \left \{ \frac{1}{x_{1}x_{2}}\cdot m, \frac{1}{y_{1}y_{2}}\cdot m \right \}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end cor-9 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
We have that
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{y_{1}y_{2}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) 
    &\iff \frac{x_{4}}{y_{1}x_{2}y_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &  (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} : P = Q_{1}, a = 2, c = 4, q = y_{1}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{2n+4}}{y_{1}x_{2}y_{2n+4}} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied to $Q_{2}$ with $a = 2n+4$, $c = 1$, and $q = x_{2}$ implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{2n+4}}{y_{1}x_{2}y_{2n+4}} \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
Similarly, it is proven that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{x_{1}x_{2}} \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- cor-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn2_structure_or_r'}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. Let $r \in J$. Let $q$ be a squarefree monomial with $\operatorname{Supp}(q) \subseteq \{x_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1,2}$. If
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{4}}{qy_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r),
\end{align*}
then $q$ is not divisible by $y_{1}$ or by $y_{2}$.
<!-- end cor-10 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied via $Q_{1}$ implies that $y_{2}$ does not divide $q$. Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{4}}{qy_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{2n+4}}{qy_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied via $Q_{2}$ implies that $y_{1}$ does not divide $q$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lem-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jn2_restriction_r'}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. Let $r \in J$. Let $q$ be a squarefree monomial with $\operatorname{Supp}(q) \subseteq \{x_{i}, y_{i}\}_{i=1,2}$. Moreover, suppose that $\#\operatorname{Supp}(q) \geq 3$. Then, 
\begin{align*}
\frac{x_{5}}{qy_{5}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
<!-- end lem-26 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
We define the elements 
\begin{align*}
    r' := \frac{x_{5}}{qy_{5}} \cdot m, \quad r'' := \frac{x_{3}}{qy_{3}} \cdot m, \quad \text{ and } \quad r''' := \frac{x_{2n+5}}{qy_{2n+5}} \cdot m.
\end{align*}
Suppose that $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$. Then, Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that $r''$ and $r'''$ also belong to $\operatorname{Supp}(r)$. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} to $r''$ via $Q_{1}$ implies that $x_{2}$ or $y_{2}$ divides $r''$. Hence, $q$ is not divisible by $x_{2}$ or by $y_{2}$. Similarly, applying Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} to $r'''$ via $Q_{2}$ implies that $x_{1}$ or $y_{1}$ divides $r'''$. Therefore, $q$ is not divisible by $x_{1}$ or by $y_{1}$. This leads to the conclusion that $\# \operatorname{Supp}(q) \leq 2$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lem-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jn2_restriction_r'_numerator}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. Let $r \in J$. For $p \in \{1,y_{1},y_{2}\}$, we have that 
\begin{align*}
\frac{p x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
<!-- end lem-27 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
When $p = 1$, we have that
\begin{align*}
    &\phantom{\iff\,\,\,} \frac{x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)\\
    &\iff \frac{x_{3}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{3}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{3}}{x_{1}y_{3}} \cdot \frac{y_{4}}{y_{2}x_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} : Q_{1}, a = 2, c = 4, d = 2n+7, p = x_{3}, q = x_{1}y_{3}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied to $Q_{2}$ with $a= 2n+4$, $c = 1$, $d = 2n+4$, $p = x_{2n+5}$, and $q = y_{2}y_{2n+5}$ implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}} \cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}

When $p = y_{1}$, we have that
\begin{align*}
     \frac{y_{1}x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
    &\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{x_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} : Q_{2}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{3}y_{4}}{x_{2}y_{3}x_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}
Lemma  \ref{lem:forbiddn_support_of_Q} applied to $Q_{1}$ with $a= 4$, $c = 2$, $d = 2n+7$, $p = x_{3}$, and $q = y_{3}$ implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{3}y_{4}}{x_{2}y_{3}x_{4}}\cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}

When $p = y_{2}$, it is shown that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{y_{2}x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{5}}\cdot m \notin \operatorname{Supp}(r)
\end{align*}
similarly as in the case where $p = y_{1}$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->

    f \cdot S &:= \{f g \mid g \in S \} \\
    S \cdot T &:= \{ a \cdot b \mid a \in S, \, b \in T \}.

<!-- lem-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. Define the ideals
\begin{align*}
    \mathfrak{a}_{0} &:= (\{x_{j}^{2},y_{j}^{2}\}_{j=6}^{2n+7}) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{1} &:= ( x_{3}^{2},y_{3}^{2}) +  ( x_{1}^{2},x_{2}^{2},y_{4}^{2},y_{5}^{2} ) + (y_{1}^{3},y_{2}^{3},x_{4}^{3}, x_{5}^{3}) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{2} &:= ( x_{1}y_{1}^{2}, x_{2}y_{2}^{2}, x_{4}^{2}y_{4}, x_{5}^{2}y_{5}  ) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{3} &:= ( x_{1}x_{2}x_{4}^{2}, x_{1}x_{2}x_{5}^{2}, x_{4}^{2}x_{5}^{2} ) \\
    \mathfrak{a}_{4} &:= ( x_{4}x_{5}y_{1}^{2}y_{4}y_{5}, x_{1}x_{4}x_{5}y_{2}^{2}y_{4}y_{5}, x_{4}x_{5}y_{1}y_{2}^{2}y_{4}y_{5}, y_{1}^{2}y_{2}^{2} ).
                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                     
\end{align*}
and $L := \sum_{i=1}^{4} \mathfrak{a}_{i}$. Let $r \in J$ and $r' \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$. If $r' \notin L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, then 
$r'$ belongs to the following set:
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{ A } \cup \mathcal{ B }
\end{align*}
where 
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{ A } &:= h_{1,1} \cdot \{1 , x_{2}, y_{1}, x_{2}y_{1} \} \cup h_{1,2} \cdot \{ 1, x_{1} , y_{2}, x_{1}y_{2} \} \cup h_{1,3} \cdot \{1,x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2},x_{1}y_{2},x_{2}y_{1}\}
    \\ 
    \mathcal{ B } &:= \{h_{2,1},h_{2,2} \} \cdot \{1,y_{1},y_{2},y_{1}y_{2} \}
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
    h_{1,1} &:= \frac{1}{x_{2}y_{1}} \cdot m 
    & h_{1,2} &:=  \frac{1}{x_{1}y_{2}} \cdot m 
    & h_{1,3} &:= \frac{x_{4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{4}} \cdot m \\
    h_{2,1} &:= \frac{x_{5}}{x_{2}y_{1}y_{5}} \cdot m
    & h_{2,2} &:= \frac{x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
<!-- end lem-28 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Since $r \in P_{i,i+2}^{[2]}:J_{G}$ for $i = 3$ and $i = 4$ and $r' \notin L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} implies that $\omega_{S} \mid r'$ for $S = [2n+7] \smallsetminus \{1,2,4,5\}$.

\underline{Case 1}. Suppose that $r{'}$ is not divisible by $x_{4}^{2}$ nor by $x_{5}^{2}$. Since $n \geq 4$, $r \in P_{2n+3,2n+5}^{[2]}:J_{G}$, and $r' \notin L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} implies that $x_{4}y_{4}x_{5}y_{5} \mid r'$. Consequently, we have that
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d'}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{x_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1,2}$. Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} applied to $r'$ via $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ implies that $d'$ is divisible by $x_{i}$ or by $y_{i}$ for both $i = 1$ and $i = 2$. After accounting for the constraint that $r'$ does not belong to $\mathfrak{a}_{1}$ nor to $\mathfrak{a}_{2}$, we see that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility_set}
    d' \in \{x_{1},y_{1},x_{1}y_{1},y_{1}^{2}\} \cdot \{ x_{2},y_{2},x_{2}y_{2},y_{2}^{2} \}.
\end{equation}
Expanding the products in   \eqref{eqn:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility_set} and removing those terms which would force $r' \in L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}$, we find that
\begin{align*}
    d' \in \{x_{1}x_{2},x_{1}y_{2}, x_{1}x_{2}y_{2} \} \cup \{y_{1}x_{2},y_{1}y_{2},y_{1}x_{2}y_{2}\} \cup \{x_{1}y_{1}x_{2},x_{1}y_{1}y_{2},x_{1}y_{1}x_{2}y_{2} \}.
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{cor:Jn2_restrictions_supp_r} implies that $d' \neq x_{1}x_{2}$ and that $d' \neq y_{1}y_{2}$. For the remaining values of $d'$ we compute that\begin{align*}
    r' \in h_{1,1} \cdot \{1 , x_{2}, y_{1}, x_{2}y_{1} \} \cup h_{1,2} \cdot \{ 1, x_{1} , y_{2}, x_{1}y_{2} \}.
\end{align*}

\underline{Case 2}. Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $x_{5}^{2}$. Since $r' \notin \mathfrak{a}_{3}$, we conclude that $r'$ is not divisible by $x_{4}^{2}$. Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} applied to $r'$ via $P_{5,7}$ implies that $x_{4}y_{4} \mid r'$. Hence we have that
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d'\cdot x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ where $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{x_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1,2}$. The fact that $y_{5} \notin \operatorname{Supp}(d')$ follows from the condition that $r' \notin \mathfrak{a}_{2}$. Suitable applications of Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} together with Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} applied to $r'$ via $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ implies that
\begin{align*}
    d' \in \{x_{1},y_{1},x_{1}y_{1},y_{1}^{2}\}\cdot \{x_{2},y_{2},x_{2}y_{2},y_{2}^{2}\}.
\end{align*}
Since $x_{1}x_{2}x_{5}^{2} \in \mathfrak{a}_{3}$, we may suppose that $x_{1} x_{2} \nmid d'$. If $y_{1}y_{2} \mid d'$ and $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{y_{1},y_{2}\}$, then 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility_impossibility}
    r' = \frac{p x_{5}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{5}}\cdot m
\end{equation}
for $p \in \{1,y_{1},y_{2}\}$. However, Lemma \ref{lem:Jn2_restriction_r'_numerator} implies that equation \eqref{eqn:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility_impossibility} is impossible. Thus, we are reduced to considering 
\begin{align*}
    d' \in \{x_{1}y_{2},x_{1}y_{2}^{2},y_{1}x_{2},y_{1}x_{2}y_{2},x_{1}y_{1}y_{2},x_{1}y_{1}y_{2}^{2},y_{1}^{2}x_{2},y_{1}^{2}x_{2}y_{2}\}.
\end{align*}
For these values of $d'$ we compute that
\begin{align*}
    r' \in \{h_{2,1},h_{2,2} \}\cdot \{1,y_{1},y_{2},y_{1}y_{2} \}.
\end{align*}

\underline{Case 3}. Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $x_{4}^{2}$ and that $r'$ is not divisible by $y_{2}^{2}$. Since $r' \notin \mathfrak{a}_{3}$, it follows that $x_{5}^{2} \nmid r'$. Since $y_{2}^{2} \nmid r'$, Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} applied to $r'$ via $Q_{1}$ implies that $x_{5}y_{5} \mid r'$. Thus, 
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' \cdot x_{4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2}y_{4}} \cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{ x_{i},y_{i} \}_{i=1,2}$. The fact that $y_{4} \notin \operatorname{Supp}(d')$ follows from the condition that $x_{4}^{2}y_{4} \in \mathfrak{a}_{2}$. Since $r'$ is not divisible by $y_{4}$, Corollary \ref{cor:Jn2_structure_or_r'} implies that $y_{1}y_{2} \mid d'$. Thus, we have that
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility_d_prime_case_3}
    d' \in \{y_{1},x_{1}y_{1},y_{1}^{2}\} \cdot \{y_{2},x_{2}y_{2},y_{2}^{2}\}.
\end{equation}
We have that $d' \neq x_{1}y_{1}x_{2}y_{2}$ (since $x_{1}x_{2} y_{4}^{2} \in \mathfrak{a}_{3}$), and we have that $d' \neq y_{1}^{2}y_{2}^{2}$ (since $y_{1}^{2}y_{2}^{2} \in \mathfrak{a}_{4}$). For the remaining values of $d'$, we compute that
\begin{align*}
    r' \in h_{1,3} \cdot \{1,x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2},x_{1}y_{2},x_{2}y_{1}\}.
\end{align*}

\underline{Case 4.} Suppose that $r'$ is divisible by $x_{4}^{2}y_{2}^{2}$. Since $r' \notin \mathfrak{a}_{2}$ it follows that $y_{4} \nmid r'$ and that $x_{2} \nmid r'$. Hence 
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' \cdot x_{4}y_{2}}{x_{1}x_{2}x_{5}y_{1}y_{4}y_{5}}\cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{ x_{1},x_{5},y_{1}, y_{5} \}$. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} to $r'$ via $P_{4,6}$ implies that 
\begin{align*}
    r'' := \frac{d' \cdot x_{6}y_{2}}{x_{1}x_{2}x_{5}y_{1}y_{6}y_{5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
Since $x_{5}^{2} \nmid d'$ (otherwise, $r' \in \mathfrak{a}_{3}$) and $y_{5}^{2} \nmid d'$ (otherwise, $r' \in \mathfrak{a}_{1}$), Lemma \ref{lem:r_in_P_div_by_omega_S} applied to $r''$ via $P_{6,8}$ implies that $x_{5}y_{5} \mid r''$. Thus, we have that
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' \cdot x_{4}y_{2}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{4}}\cdot m
\end{align*}
for some monomial $d'$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(d') \subseteq \{ x_{1},y_{1} \}$. Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that 
\begin{align*}
    r''' := \frac{d' \cdot x_{2n+4}y_{2}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
We observe that $y_{1}^{2} \nmid r'''$ (otherwise, $r' \in \mathfrak{a}_{4}$), $y_{2n+4}\nmid r'''$, and $y_{2n+6}^{2} \nmid r'''$. Consequently, Lemma \ref{lem:supp_Q_div_bin_supp} applied to $r'''$ via $Q_{2}$ implies that $y_{1}$ divides $r'''$. Thus, $y_{1} \mid d'$, and we have that
\begin{align*}
    r' = \frac{d' \cdot x_{4}y_{2}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{4}}\cdot m
\end{align*}
for some $d' \in \{1,x_{1}\}$. For $d' \in \{1,x_{1}\}$, we have that 
\begin{align*}
    r' \in h_{1,3} \cdot \{y_{2},x_{1}y_{2}\}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lem-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jn2_two_elts_in_supp_r}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. Let $r \in J$ and $p \in \{1,y_{1},y_{2},y_{1}y_{2}\}$. Then,
\begin{align*}
    \frac{p  x_{5}}{x_{2}y_{1}y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{p x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
<!-- end lem-29 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
When $p \in \{1,y_{1}\}$, we have that 
\begin{align*}
    &\phantom{\iff\,\,\,\,} \frac{px_{5}}{x_{2}y_{1}y_{5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)\\
    &\iff \frac{px_{3}}{x_{2}y_{1}y_{3}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling}) \\
    &\iff \frac{px_{3}y_{4}}{y_{1}y_{2}y_{3}x_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} : Q_{1}, p' = px_{3}, q' = y_{1}y_{3}, a = 2, c = 4) \\
    &\iff \frac{py_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{y_{1}y_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}

Specializing to the case that $p = 1$, we have that
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_two_elts_in_supp_r_0}
    \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{y_{1}y_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
    \iff \frac{x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
\end{equation}
by applying Lemma \ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} to $Q_{2}$ with $p' = x_{2n+5}$, $q' = y_{2}y_{2n+5}$, $a = 1$, and $c = 2n+4$. Finally, Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} applied to equation \eqref{eqn:Jn2_two_elts_in_supp_r_0} implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}

Specializing to the case that $p = y_{1}$, we have that
\begin{align*}
    &\phantom{\iff\,\,\,\,} \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{y_{2}x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)\\
    &\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} : Q_{2}, p' = x_{2n+5}, q' = y_{2}y_{2n+5}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{2}y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}). \\
\end{align*}

\underline{Case $p = y_{2}$:} The proof is analogous to the case where $p = y_{1}$.

\underline{Case $p = y_{1}y_{2}$:} 
We have that
\begin{align*}
\frac{y_{2}x_{5}}{x_{2}y_{5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) 
&\iff \frac{y_{2}x_{3}}{x_{2}y_{3}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling}) \\
&\iff \frac{y_{4}x_{3}}{x_{4}y_{3}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} : Q_{1}) \\
&\iff \frac{y_{2n+4}x_{2n+5}}{x_{2n+4}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
&\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+5}}{x_{1}y_{2n+5}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} : Q_{2}) \\
&\iff \frac{y_{1}x_{5}}{x_{1}y_{5}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lem-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jn2_three_elts_in_supp_r}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. We utilize notation as introduced in Lemma \ref{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}. Let $r \in J$, then 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $h_{1,1} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $h_{1,2} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $h_{1,3} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$,
    \item $x_{1} h_{1,2} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $x_{1} h_{1,3} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$,
    \item $y_{1} h_{1,1} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $y_{1} h_{1,3} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$,
    \item $x_{2} h_{1,1} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $x_{2} h_{1,3} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$, and
    \item $y_{2} h_{1,2} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$ if and only if $y_{2} h_{1,3} \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-30 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
(1) First, we observe that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{x_{1}y_{2}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{x_{4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
\end{align*}
by applying Lemma \ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} to $h_{1,2}$ with $Q_{1}$ and $p = 1$, $q = x_{1}$, $a = 2$, $c = 4$, and $d = 2n+7$.
Next, we observe that 
\begin{align*}
    &\phantom{\iff\,\,\,\,} \frac{1}{x_{2}y_{1}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{2n+4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q} : Q_{2}, p = 1, q = x_{2}, a = 1, c = 2n+4) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{4}} \cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}

The proof of statements (2) and (4) are similar to the proof of (1), and we do not repeat these proofs.

The proof of statement (3) is similar to the proof of (5). Thus, we give the proof of (5) below. We have that
\begin{align*}
    y_{2}h_{1,2} = \frac{1}{x_{1}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
    &\iff \frac{y_{2n+4}}{y_{1}x_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q}:\; Q_{2}, a=1,c= 2n+4) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2}}{y_{1}x_{2}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q} : Q_{1}) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2}x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:elements_in_supp_of_Q}:\; Q_{2}, a=1, c = 2n+4) \\
    &\iff \frac{y_{2}x_{4}}{x_{1}x_{2}y_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & & (\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- cor-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:Jn2_supp_r_exclusivity}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. We utilize notation as introduced in Lemma \ref{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}. Let $r \in J$, then
\begin{align*}
    \left \lvert  \{m, x_{1}y_{2}h_{1,3}, x_{2}y_{1}h_{1,3}\} \cap \operatorname{Supp}(r)   \right\rvert \equiv 0 \mod{2}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end cor-11 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:Jn_m_in_Supp_f} applied to $Q_{2}$ implies that
\begin{align*}
    \left \lvert  \{m, \frac{x_{1}y_{2n+4}}{y_{1}x_{2n+4}}\cdot m, \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}y_{2n+4}}\cdot m \} \cap \operatorname{Supp}(r)  \right\rvert \equiv 0 \mod{2}.
\end{align*}
Lemma \ref{lem:cycling} implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{y_{1}x_{2n+4}}{x_{1}y_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) \iff \frac{y_{1}x_{4}}{x_{1}y_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r).
\end{align*}
We observe that
\begin{align*}
    \frac{x_{1}y_{2n+4}}{y_{1}x_{2n+4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r)
    &\iff \frac{x_{1}y_{4}}{y_{1}x_{4}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{1}y_{2}}{y_{1}x_{2}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q}: Q_{1}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{2n+4}y_{2}}{y_{2n+4}x_{2}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling_via_Q}: Q_{2}) \\
    &\iff \frac{x_{4}y_{2}}{y_{4}x_{2}}\cdot m \in \operatorname{Supp}(r) & &(\ref{lem:cycling} \text{ iteratively})
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Jn2_J_contained_in_Q}
Let the setup be as in \ref{setup:Jn2}. We utilize notation as introduced in Lemma \ref{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}. Then,
\begin{align*}
    J + L + \mathfrak{a}_{0} \subseteq ( h_{1,1} + h_{1,2} + h_{1,3}, h_{2,1} + h_{2,2} ) + L + \mathfrak{a}_{0}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Let $r \in J$. Let $S := \operatorname{Supp}(r) \smallsetminus (L+\mathfrak{a}_{0})$. Define the sets
\begin{align*}
    S_{1} &= \{h_{1,1},h_{1,2},h_{1,3}\} & S_{6} &= \{ m,x_{1}y_{2}h_{1,3} \} & S_{9} &= \{ h_{2,1}, h_{2,2} \}  \\
    S_{2} &= \{x_{1} h_{1,2}, x_{1} h_{1,3}\} &  S_{7} &= \{ m,x_{2}y_{1}h_{1,3} \} & S_{10} &= \{ y_{1}h_{2,1}, y_{1}h_{2,2} \} \\
    S_{3} &= \{y_{1} h_{1,1}, y_{1} h_{1,3}\} &  S_{8} &= \{ x_{1}y_{2}h_{1,3}, x_{2}y_{1}h_{1,3} \} & S_{11} &= \{ y_{2}h_{2,1}, y_{2}h_{2,2} \} \\
    S_{4} &= \{x_{2} h_{1,1}, x_{2} h_{1,3}\} & & & S_{12} &= \{ y_{1}y_{2}h_{2,1}, y_{1}y_{2}h_{2,2} \} \\
    S_{5} &= \{y_{2} h_{1,2}, y_{2} h_{1,3}\} 
\end{align*}
Then, Lemmas \ref{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}, \ref{lem:Jn2_two_elts_in_supp_r}, \ref{lem:Jn2_three_elts_in_supp_r}, and \ref{cor:Jn2_supp_r_exclusivity} imply that there exists $1 \leq t \leq 12$ and $1 \leq i_{1} < \cdots < i_{t} \leq 12$ satisfying $\# \left( \{i_{1},\ldots,i_{t}\} \cap \{6,7,8\} \right) \leq 1$ such that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_reln_1}
    S = S_{i_{1}} \sqcup \cdots \sqcup S_{i_{t}}.
\end{equation}
We observe that for the elements of $S_{2}$ that we have the relation 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_reln_2}
    x_{1} (h_{1,1} + h_{1,2} + h_{1,3}) = x_{1} h_{1,2} + x_{1} h_{1,3} \mod{(L + \mathfrak{a}_{0})}.
\end{equation}
A similar relation holds for the elements of $S_{i}$ for $3 \leq i \leq 7$. The elements of $S_{8}$ satisfy the relation
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:Jn2_reln_3}
    (x_{1}y_{2} + x_{2}y_{1})(h_{1,1} + h_{1,2} + h_{1,3}) = x_{1}y_{2}h_{1,3} + x_{2}y_{1}h_{1,3} \mod{(L + \mathfrak{a}_{0})}.
\end{equation}
It follows that
\begin{align*}
    r = \sum_{j = 1}^{t} \sum_{g\in S_{i_{j}}} g \mod{(L + \mathfrak{a}_{0})}.
\end{align*}
Now, equations \eqref{eqn:Jn2_reln_2} and \eqref{eqn:Jn2_reln_3} imply that
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{g\in S_{i_{j}}} g \in (h_{1,1}+h_{1,2}+h_{1,3},h_{2,1} + h_{2,2}),
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- thrm-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:Jn2_not_F_pure}
Let $n\geq 0$ be a positive integer, and $G$ the graph $\mathrm{co\!-\!XF}_6^{2n+2}$. Then, $J_{G}$ is not F-pure.
<!-- end thrm-13 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
When $n = 0$ and $n = 1$, it can be verified via Macaulay2 that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure. Hence, it suffices to consider the cases $n \geq 3$. We utilize the notation for $h_{i,j}$ and $L$ as they are defined in Lemma \ref{lem:Jn2_supp_r_divisibility}. We will use Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} to prove that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure. Adopting the notation from Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} we have that $A = \{2n+6,2n+7\}$, $B = [2n+7] \smallsetminus (A\cup \{1,2\})$, $Q = P(A,B)$, $m = 7$, $B' = [7] \smallsetminus \{1,2\}$, $Q' = P(\varnothing,B')$. We define the ideal
\begin{align*}
    K := ( h_{1,1} + h_{1,2} + h_{1,3}, h_{2,1} + h_{2,2} ) + L + (\{ x_{i}^{2},y_{i}^{2} \}_{i=6,7} ).
\end{align*}
We define $\mathcal{ C } := \{P_{i,i+2} \mid 3 \leq i \leq 2n+3\}\cup \{Q_{i} \mid i \in \{1,2\}\}$. Proposition \ref{prop:Jn2_J_contained_in_Q} implies that the containment  \eqref{eqn:reduction_step_fedder_computation_assumption_1} of Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} is satisfied. We verify using Macaulay2 that the containment \eqref{eqn:reduction_step_fedder_computation_assumption_2} of Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} is satisfied. Thus, Proposition \ref{prop:reduction_step_fedder_computation} implies that $J_{G}$ is not F-pure.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
$S = \Bbbk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and let $I \subseteq S$ be a graded ideal of height $h$. We say that $I$ is of \textbf{K\"onig type}, if there exists a sequence $\underline{f} = f_1,\ldots,f_h$ of homogeneous polynomials
that form part of a minimal system of generators of $I$ and a monomial order $<$
on $S$ such that $\mathrm{in}_<(f_1),\ldots,\mathrm{in}_<(f_h)$ is a regular sequence.
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- thrm-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:bei_konig_type}
Let $G$ be a graph. Then, $J_{G}$ is of K\"onig type if and only if $G$ contains vertex disjoint paths $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{t}$ such that 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^{t} \left \lvert E(P_{i}) \right\rvert = \operatorname{ht} J_{G}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end thrm-14 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:konig_unmixed_bei_F_pure}
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices. Let $J_{G}$ be an unmixed ideal of K\"onig type. If the characteristic of the base field is $p >0$, then $R_{G}$ is F-pure.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Let $P_{1},\ldots,P_{t}$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:bei_konig_type}. Let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{g}$ denote the binomials corresponding to the edges of the $P_{i}$, where $g = \operatorname{ht} J_{G}$. By {\cite[Corollary 3.3]{pandey2024linkage}}, if $R/\mathfrak{a}$ is F-injective, where $\mathfrak{a} = (\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{g})$, then $R/J_{G}$ is F-pure as $\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{g}$ form a regular sequence in $J_G$ of length $\operatorname{ht} J_{G}$. The ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ is even F-pure. Since the $\alpha_{i}$ form a regular sequence, it follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:reg:sequence} that
\begin{align*}
    \mathfrak{a}^{[p]} : \mathfrak{a} = \left( \prod_{i=1}^{g} \alpha_{i}^{p-1} \right) + \mathfrak{a}^{[p]}.
\end{align*}
The lead term of $\prod_{i=1}^{g} \alpha_{i}^{p-1}$ with respect to the lexicographic term order induced by $x_{1} > x_{2} > \cdots > x_{n} > y_{1} > y_{2} > \cdots > y_{n}$ does not belong to $\mathfrak{m}^{[p]}$. Thus, 
\begin{align*}
    \mathfrak{a}^{[p]}:\mathfrak{a} \not \subseteq \mathfrak{m}^{[p]}.
\end{align*}
Hence, Fedder's criterion (Theorem \ref{thm:fedder_criterion}) implies that $R/\mathfrak{a}$ is F-pure.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- cor-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:unmixed_Konig_type_are_wc}
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices. Suppose that the binomial edge ideal $J_{G}$ is an unmixed ideal of K\"onig type. Then $G$ is weakly closed.
<!-- end cor-12 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Note that $J_{G}$ being unmixed (resp., of K\"onig type) are combinatorial statements independent of the base field; see, for instance, Proposition \ref{prop:min_primes_binomial_edge_ideal} (resp., \cite{laclair2023invariants}). Hence, we may assume that the base field has characteristic $2$. Proposition \ref{prop:konig_unmixed_bei_F_pure} implies that $R_{G}$ is F-pure, and Theorem \ref{thm:matsudas_conjecture_is_true} implies that $G$ is weakly closed.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- ques-1: body_md -->
If $G$ is a graph which is weakly closed (with $J_{G}$ unmixed), then is $J_{G}$ of K\"onig type?
<!-- end ques-1 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:exact_sequence_binomial_edge_ideal}
Let $G$ be a graph and $v \in G$ a non-simplicial vertex. Then, there is a short exact sequence of $R$-modules
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:ses_binomial_edge_ideal}
    0 \rightarrow R/J_{G} \rightarrow R/J_{G_{v}} \oplus R_{v}/J_{G \smallsetminus v} \rightarrow R_{v}/J_{G_{v} \smallsetminus v} \rightarrow 0
\end{equation}
where $R_{v} = \Bbbk[X_{i},Y_{i} : i \in [n] \smallsetminus \{v\}]$.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:wc_preserved_under_completion_deletion}
Let $G$ be a weakly closed graph, and $v$ a vertex of $G$. Then the graphs $G \smallsetminus v$, $G_{v}$, and $G_{v} \smallsetminus v$ are weakly closed.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Since $G$ is a weakly closed graph, $R_{G}$ is F-pure whenever the base field $\Bbbk$ has characteristic two (Theorem \ref{thm:weakly_closed_are_F_pure}). Lemma \ref{lem:F_pure_preserved_vertex_deletion_completion} implies that $G \smallsetminus v$, $G_{v}$, and $G_{v} \smallsetminus v$ define F-pure binomial edge ideals. Since the base field has characteristic two, Theorem \ref{thm:matsudas_conjecture_is_true} implies that the graphs $G \smallsetminus v$, $G_{v}$, and $G_{v} \smallsetminus v$ are all weakly closed.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
